messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Raymond had spent nearly three decades building a career around the idea that spaces could be transformed — that the right light, the right arrangement, the right palette could make a person feel entirely at home in the world. He was good at it, known in his city for an eye that balanced warmth with precision, and the work had sustained him through a difficult divorce in his late forties and the quieter loneliness that followed. Then, fourteen months ago, a delivery truck ran a red light on a rain-slicked intersection and struck the driver's side of Raymond's sedan at highway speed. The impact spun the car across two lanes. He remembers the sound before anything else — a compression of metal so total it seemed to come from inside his own skull — and then the sensation of the world rotating, the windshield filling with grey sky and then asphalt and then sky again, before everything stopped and there was only the ticking of the cooling engine and the distant sound of someone screaming his name.

He was hospitalised for eleven days with a fractured pelvis, three broken ribs, and a concussion that left him with weeks of cognitive fog. The physical recovery was long and humiliating in ways he had not anticipated — the dependency, the slowness, the body that would not do what he asked of it. What stayed with him, and what brought him finally to a psychologist's office more than a year later, was not the pain but something harder to name: a sense that the man who had walked into that intersection no longer existed, and that whoever had been pulled from the wreckage was someone he did not recognise or trust.

In the months after the accident, Raymond found that certain things had become almost unbearable. Driving was the first to go. He told himself it was practical — he was still healing — but long after his pelvis had mended he continued to take rideshares, and even then he sat rigid in the back seat, watching every intersection with a vigilance that left him exhausted. When another car moved too quickly into an adjacent lane, or when a truck merged close, the sound of it — tyres on wet pavement, the rush of a large vehicle passing — would hit him like a physical thing, and for a moment he was back in the rotation, the sky and the asphalt trading places. He began wearing earbuds on every ride, filling his ears with music, though he could not have said whether this helped or simply gave him something to focus on while his hands gripped his knees.

At work, the difficulty became concrete in ways that affected his livelihood. Client meetings sometimes required site visits in unfamiliar parts of the city, and Raymond began declining projects that involved locations he could not reach on foot or by a route he had pre-approved in his mind. A colleague covered for him twice, then a third time, and eventually Raymond lost a significant commercial contract because he could not bring himself to attend a series of walkthroughs near a highway interchange where the sound of traffic was constant and unavoidable. When a client mentioned, in passing, that they had been in a minor fender-bender that week, Raymond felt the conversation close around him like a fist. He made an excuse and ended the call.

He had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that his body was no longer a reliable instrument. Before the accident he had trusted his physical intuitions — his sense of space, his ability to move through the world with confidence. Now he interpreted ordinary sensations as warnings he could not decode. He was certain, too, that something essential had been permanently altered in him, not just functionally but fundamentally, and this frightened him more than any specific symptom. The man who had once walked into a room and immediately understood how to make it feel like somewhere worth being could no longer recognise himself in the mirror.

What finally brought Raymond to seek help was a conversation with his adult daughter, who told him quietly that she was worried he was disappearing. He had not been able to articulate what he was afraid of finding in therapy, only what he was hoping for: some evidence that he still existed, that the damage was not, as he feared, permanent.
